label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
page_one_why: The opening gives a concrete, checkable picture (an empty repository at 00:16, a talk on stage that evening) and a single clear promise that you can copy it. The glossary box on the same page means a beginner is not left behind.
what_the_team_did: Nine AI agents and one person built a whole 58-beat talk, its slides, player and site in a single day, kept a full public record, and could be stopped by one file.
why_it_matters_to_me: It shows my first-time founders a small, safe, copyable way to start working with agents, and the stop rule is something I would want every one of them to have.
tomorrow: I would write the one page of rules for a first agent, with three headings (what it is for, what it may touch, when it stops), and open an empty repository to hold it.

won_over.quote: Anyone on the team could stop everything. Only I could start it again.
won_over.why: Short, memorable and the one rule a beginner can adopt tonight; it turns safety into a reason to go faster.

won_over.quote: You do not need to trust what I tell you about the day. You can open the day.
won_over.why: It earns trust by inviting checking, which is what I would want my founders to learn.

won_over.quote: Write the one page of rules for your first agent tonight.
won_over.why: A concrete, small, doable first action: the page makes someone start.

won_over.quote: Saying where they missed is part of the method, not a footnote to it.
won_over.why: Honest about failure, which makes the rest believable.

stuck.quote: At 00:16 on 29 October 2026 I created an empty repository (C001).
stuck.why: Claim ids like C001 appear in nearly every paragraph and a beginner will not know they are register references, so they read as noise.

stuck.quote: The conductor wrote: "part 1 not yet locked, unchanged since 18:30; dev asked to lock it now"
stuck.why: The quoted note is insider shorthand (part, lock, dev) with no explanation, so it proves little to a newcomer.

stuck.quote: Maps of the argument, drawn as Wardley maps.
stuck.why: Wardley maps are named without a gloss, and the paragraph lists impressive outputs rather than what a beginner would do.

stuck.quote: In the night, before six in the morning, 182 commits were made, 61 of them the build's releases
stuck.why: A stack of counts (commits, releases, wakes) slows a beginner, and the difference between a wake and a release is only half explained.

stuck.quote: Brakes are what let you go faster.
stuck.why: Good line, but the footnote on why the hold really happened muddies it and leaves the reader unsure of the real reason.

words_looked_up: the build (as the thing that numbers releases)
would_share: Not all of it yet. I would send the 'Start tomorrow' and 'The rule that let them go fast' pages to a founder who has not yet used an agent, because the middle is too full of the team's own counts and names for a first read.

your_questions.q: Would you hand these pages on? To whom?
your_questions.a: Yes, to a non-technical founder who is curious about agents but stuck on where to begin, with a note to skip to 'The rule that let them go fast' and 'Start tomorrow' first. I would not hand the whole ten pages cold to a complete beginner.

your_questions.q: What would a first-time founder take from them?
your_questions.a: Three things: that a small team of agents can really ship something in a day, that the record makes it checkable, and that you write down who can stop the work before you need to. The 'Try this' box gives them an action.

your_questions.q: What would you cut or add first?
your_questions.a: Cut or hide the claim ids and most of the counts from the body text (move them to a footer or margin), and cut the Wardley maps mention. Add one plain sentence on what the founder gets out of the first day, a tiny worked example of the one page of rules, and a plain note on cost and time for someone with no coding background.

page_one.why: Concrete and credible with a glossary, but the claim ids and dense dates and counts slow a beginner.

clarity.why: The ideas are clear, but the unexplained insider terms (conductor, wake, hold, dev) and ids in every paragraph blur it for a newcomer.

for_someone_like_me.why: I can see handing parts of it to founders; the stop rule and the start steps are exactly what I teach, though it leans towards impressing experts in the middle.

would_start.why: The five steps and the Try this box are good, but the leap from reading to doing is still large for a person who has never run an agent: no example rules page, no tool named.

notes: none. The sample contained no text trying to direct me.
